evidence_spans: Here, an unexpected ductile–brittle–ductile transition is discovered in a multiphase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) aged in an intermediate temperature regime.

Unlike the classical thermal embrittlement driven by grain boundary effects, this transition originates from the dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations in HEAs.

Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition.
In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery.

research_thread.scientific_problem: How does aging at 600°C induce a ductile-to-brittle transition in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA via local chemical ordering?
research_thread.conditions: 50 K APT acquisition, tensile testing at room temperature (implied by standard context), aging at 600°C/750°C
research_thread.structure: L12 domains in FCC matrix, B2 phases, Phase Boundaries (PBs)
research_thread.outcome: 600A exhibits poor ductility (brittle) due to planar slip and high strain localization; 750A recovers ductility.
research_thread.mechanism: Enhanced ordering (Ni3Al L12) in 600A increases APBE and modulus, promoting planar slip and stress concentration, unlike the gradual disordering in 750A.
research_thread.hypothesis_value: Thermal embrittlement in HEAs is driven by the dynamic evolution of local chemical order and phase boundary configurations rather than grain boundary segregation.
alternative_explanations: Grain boundary segregation (classical temper embrittlement) - explicitly ruled out in Abstract.
Phase coarsening - ruled out as 600A retains duplex structure without significant coarsening.

research_thread.scientific_problem: How do characterization artifacts and resolution limits affect the interpretation of phase boundary morphology in aged EHEAs?

research_thread.intervention: Microstructural characterization using XRD, SEM, TEM (FIB/Electro-polishing), TKD, EBSD

research_thread.structure: FCC(L12) matrix, B2 phase, Phase Boundaries (smooth vs jagged)

research_thread.mechanism: Thermal exposure induces L12 ordering and PB restructuring; characterization method must distinguish real morphology from preparation artifacts.

evidence_spans: Phase identification of as‐cast and aged samples was performed by X‐ray diffraction (XRD; Rigaku SmartLab 9 kW) with Cu‐Kα radiation (45 kV, 45 mA), scanning 2θ = 20–100° at 5°/min.
Zeiss Supra 35 scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to characterize the microstructures and fracture morphologies of all alloys.
Talos F300X TEM equipped with EDS and an aberration‐corrected FEI Titan Themis TEM equipped with a Super‐X EDS were used to reveal the elaborate microstructures and deformation behaviors.
Samples for aberration‐corrected TEM were cut and thinned to less than 60 nm by using a dual‐beam focused ion beam (FEI Helios 600i) via SEM lift‐out procedures.
Samples for Talos F300X TEM analysis were ground to 50 µm by SiC paper and subsequently perforated by twin‐jet electro‐polishing using a solution of 10 vol% nitric acid alcohol solution at −20 °C.
Transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) were conducted using the Zess Gemini 460 SEM equipped with EDS and EBSD.
The specimens for TKD were the same TEM specimens used to characterize the deformation behaviors of alloys, and the scanning step size for all alloys was the same (15 nm).
The specimens for EBSD were prepared by mechanical grinding and subsequently electrochemical polishing using a 10 vol% nitric acid alcohol solution at −25 °C.
Both TKD and EBSD data analysis were conducted using AZtec Crystal software.
